title: Exothermic process
body: A process in which the energy of the system decreases because the system loses energy to the surroundings as heat transfer from, or work done by, the system.
ced_evidence: 6.1.A.3 "the energy of the system either decreases (exothermic reaction)"

title: Endothermic process
body: A process in which the energy of the system increases because the system gains energy from the surroundings as heat transfer to, or work done on, the system.
ced_evidence: 6.1.A.3 "increases (endothermic reaction)"

title: Solution formation can be exothermic or endothermic
body: Dissolving is exothermic or endothermic depending on the relative strengths of the intermolecular/interparticle interactions before and after dissolution.
caution: Justify the claim by comparing interaction strengths before and after dissolving, not just by stating the temperature change.
ced_evidence: 6.1.A.4 "depending on the relative strengths of intermolecular/interparticle interactions"

title: Ways a chemical system changes its energy
body: The three main processes by which chemical systems change their energy (also the processes named as endothermic/exothermic examples).

items.label: Heating/cooling
items.meaning: Heating raises the system's energy; cooling lowers it.

items.label: Phase transitions
items.meaning: Melting and boiling raise the system's energy; freezing and condensing lower it.

items.label: Chemical reactions
items.meaning: The system's energy decreases (exothermic) or increases (endothermic).

ced_evidence: 6.4.A.6 "heating/cooling, phase transitions, and chemical reactions"

title: Energy diagram for a physical or chemical process
body: A diagram that shows whether a process is endothermic or exothermic by comparing the energy of the starting and ending states.

items.label: Energy axis
items.meaning: The vertical axis, labelled with energy and units.

items.label: Reactants (initial state) level
items.meaning: Energy of the system before the process.

items.label: Products (final state) level
items.meaning: Energy of the system after the process.

items.label: Direction of change
items.meaning: Products lower than reactants means exothermic; products higher means endothermic.

ced_evidence: 6.2.A.1 "energy diagram that shows the endothermic or exothermic nature of that process"

title: Heat transfer (heat exchange)
body: The transfer of energy that results from collisions between particles in thermal contact, also called "transfer of energy as heat."
ced_evidence: 6.3.A.2 "Collisions between particles in thermal contact can result in the transfer of energy"

title: Thermal equilibrium
body: The state reached through continued particle collisions in which two bodies have the same average kinetic energy and therefore the same temperature.
caution: The warmer body's particles have greater average kinetic energy before equilibrium; explain in terms of particle collisions and average kinetic energy.
ced_evidence: 6.3.A.3 "the average kinetic energy of both bodies is the same, and hence, their temperatures are the same"

title: Heat transfer equation
body: q = mc\Delta T
caution: Use the mass of the whole substance whose temperature changes (e.g., total solution mass, not just the solute mass), and attend to significant figures.
ced_evidence: 6.4.A.1 "EQN: q = mcΔT"

title: Specific heat capacity vs. molar heat capacity
body: Both are heat capacities used in energy calculations; specific heat capacity is per mass of substance (c in q = mcΔT) and molar heat capacity is per mole.
ced_evidence: 6.4.A.5 "specific heat capacity of a substance and the molar heat capacity are both used in energy calculations"

title: First law of thermodynamics
body: Energy is conserved in chemical and physical processes.
ced_evidence: 6.4.A.2 "energy is conserved in chemical and physical processes"

title: Equal heat does not give equal temperature change
body: The same amount of thermal energy transferred to equal masses of substances with different specific heat capacities produces different temperature changes.
ced_evidence: 6.4.A.3 "will not produce the same temperature change in equal masses of matter with differing specific heat capacities"

title: Reading dissolution calorimetry temperature changes
body: If the mixture's temperature increases, the dissolution is exothermic (energy released); if it decreases, the dissolution is endothermic (energy absorbed).
ced_evidence: 6.4.A.7 "If the temperature of the mixture increases, thermal energy is released by the dissolution process (exothermic)"

title: Heat from moles and molar enthalpy
body: q = n\,\Delta H_{\text{molar}}
caution: Sign matters: q is positive when energy is absorbed (melting, boiling, endothermic reaction) and negative when released.
ced_evidence: 6.5.A / 6.6.A "amount of the substance in moles and the molar enthalpy"

title: Phase changes: energy direction and constant temperature
body: Melting and boiling absorb energy (system energy increases), freezing and condensing release energy, and a pure substance's temperature stays constant during a phase change.
ced_evidence: 6.5.A.1 "The temperature of a pure substance remains constant during a phase change"

title: Complementary phase changes have opposite enthalpies
body: The energy absorbed in one phase change equals the energy released in the reverse change, so molar enthalpy of condensation is the negative of molar enthalpy of vaporization (and freezing is the negative of fusion).
ced_evidence: 6.5.A.2 "molar enthalpy of condensation of a substance is equal to the negative of its molar enthalpy of vaporization"

title: Sign of enthalpy change of reaction
body: A negative ΔH means heat is released by the reaction (exothermic); a positive ΔH means heat is absorbed (endothermic), at constant pressure.
caution: A measured temperature increase in the surroundings means the reaction is exothermic, so ΔH must be reported as negative.
ced_evidence: 6.6.A.1 "released (for negative values) or absorbed (for positive values)"

title: Direction of thermal energy flow in a reaction
body: In an exothermic reaction thermal energy flows to the surroundings as reactants become products; in an endothermic reaction it flows from the surroundings.
ced_evidence: 6.6.A.2 "Thermal energy is transferred to the surroundings as the reactants convert to products in an exothermic reaction"

title: Enthalpy of reaction from average bond energies
body: \Delta H_{\text{reaction}} \approx \Sigma(\text{bond energies of bonds broken}) - \Sigma(\text{bond energies of bonds formed})
caution: Count every bond broken in all reactant molecules and every bond formed in all product molecules, using the balanced equation's coefficients. Energy released greater than energy required means exothermic.
ced_evidence: 6.7.A.2 "adding up the average bond energies of all the bonds in the reactant molecules"

title: Standard enthalpy of reaction from enthalpies of formation
body: \Delta H^{\circ}_{\text{reaction}} = \Sigma \Delta H_f^{\circ}{}_{\text{products}} - \Sigma \Delta H_f^{\circ}{}_{\text{reactants}}
ced_evidence: 6.8.A.1 "EQN: ΔH°reaction = ΣΔHf °products − ΣΔHf °reactants"

title: Essential principles of Hess's law
body: Three rules for manipulating reactions and their enthalpy changes to obtain an overall reaction.

items.label: Reverse a reaction
items.meaning: ΔH keeps the same magnitude but its sign is reversed.

items.label: Multiply a reaction by a factor c
items.meaning: ΔH is multiplied by the same factor c.

items.label: Add reactions to get an overall reaction
items.meaning: The individual ΔH values are added to give the net ΔH of the overall reaction.

caution: Check that the manipulated equations actually sum to the target overall equation before adding the ΔH values.
ced_evidence: 6.9.B.2 "essential principles of Hess's law"

title: Enthalpy of an overall process equals the sum of its steps
body: At constant pressure, the enthalpy change of the overall process equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of the individual steps because total energy is conserved.
ced_evidence: 6.9.B.1 "the enthalpy change of the overall process is equal to the sum of the enthalpy changes of the individual steps"
